content:
I've worked in an org where pair programming was expected by everyone. Each major task was supposed to be done by a pair of devs. They were given freedom to decide how to breakup the task and reach the finish line through pair programming.

Here are my experiences:

1. It is incredibly exhausting. After couple of hours of continuous screen-sharing call with my pair, I used to get tired and I had to continue with it if I don't want to handover the remaining task to my pair.

2. One of my pair was rude and they used to get frustrated over little things. For example, if they want me to navigate to few files to review some code and if I overscroll a bit or don't use keyboard shortcuts to jump to a line, they showed frustration.

3. It put me under immense pressure to keep up with my pair always. I was alert all the time, not trying to make any obvious mistakes, pushing myself trying to think faster than my pair.

4. I'm not a fast thinker. My pair was. They had higher understanding of the codebase and I was few months old in the project and the org. This is an issue as well. The pair would want me to write some code because they thought of an approach before I could. Since it is their approach, they have higher understanding about it and I had to just follow their instructions to see how it turns out. Even when I am not sure about the practicality of their approach, I had no option but to continue listening to them and write the code they dictate. I hated it so much.

5. When completing any task through pair programming, I didn't get any satisfaction which I used to get when I achieved the completion of task by myself. I felt my pair had more contribution to the task compared to me. I hated that feeling.

6. In a team, the teammates are of varying work experiences. We can't expect them to match the thinking speed of each other while working in a pair. We can't expect them to match the code writing speed of each other while working on a pair.

content:
I'm a big fan of pair programming and I hate that it's so rare in the industry. I get that it's not for everyone. But I think the biggest problem for pair programming is that no one really knows what they're doing. Most of the time companies just throw a senior and a junior together and tell them to "pair", but no one has any real practice pairing.

Pairing works best when there's a formal method involved. "Extreme Programming" had some formalized rules for how to handle pair programming, like the more experienced dev being the "navigator", and the less experienced dev being the "driver", or the guidelines they had around gauging when pairing was no longer productive. My personal experience leads me to believe it's best when time boxed to an hour or two. It's not an all day thing.

It's also heavily dependent on the people involved and the work being done. Not all work is a great candidate for pair programming, and not all devs can pair well together. Some may not handle pair programming well in any situation. But if it's something you've tried and it hasn't worked, I wouldn't assume it's because pair programming just doesn't work for you. It's still worth trying on different projects, or with different people, or with a different method.

content:
I'm not familiar with RIPEMD, but some things I noted scanning the article:

> \#define F2(x, y, z) vorrq_u32(vandq_u32(x, y), vandq_u32(vmvnq_u32(x), z))

Use BIC instead of AND+MVN.  Actually, you'll notice that this is a bit-select, so you can replace the whole thing with BSL (and do the same for F4).  
Similarly, use ORN instead of ORR+MVN.

> \#define ROTL(x, n) vorrq_u32(vshlq_n_u32(x, n), vshrq_n_u32(x, 32 - (n)))

ARM does have SRI (shift-right and insert), which reduces the rotate from the 3 operations above, to 2.

> Instead, it should be written in vaddq_u32(vec1, vdupq_n_u32(2)) style (if anyone knows why this is the case – please leave a comment).

Actually MUL is the exception, as there's an instruction which allows multiplying by a single element (probably aimed at accelerating matrix multiplication).  SIMD in general operates on vectors, so you need to be passing everything in as one.  It's possible that they make shortcut intrinsics (like SVE does), but behind the scenes, it's broadcasting a scalar to a vector and adding it.

> w[i] = vld1q_u32(((uint32_t[4]){x[0][i], x[1][i], x[2][i], x[3][i]})); // A bit faster

Generally you want to arrange your data to avoid needing this interleaving (i.e. do `x[16][4]` instead of `x[4][16]`) - see [SoA layout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AoS_and_SoA).  If you can't rearrange your data, using LD4 will be faster than inserting items in lane by lane, though I don't think that can be done with a 16x4 layout, so it'd be better to transpose via TRN1 etc.

> This is a great result, but it's unfortunate that M-chips don't have SVE for 256/512 bits (8/16 lanes), as that would make it even better!

Not necessarily.  The width of a vector doesn't necessarily map to the execution unit width (e.g. Neoverse V1 declares 256-bit SVE but uses 128-bit EUs).  Though it can help if you're not making good use of ILP (which you might not be here, as it looks like you're only processing one vector at a time).  
You can process 8 hashes at a time with NEON - just use two vectors instead of one.

> It's a mystery to me why it works this way, and maybe there is an even more effective arrangement. Who knows? Please, write in the comments.

My guess is that you're exploiting [ILP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instruction-level_parallelism) better.  If the left and right rounds are independent, you want to interleave them, as it allows the processor to execute both parts simultaneously.  IIRC the M1 has 4 SIMD ports (M2 probably is the same) and you want to fill all of them for best performance.

> What's interesting is that AVX2 on the Intel N100 runs 20% faster than Neon on the Apple M2 (mainly because of the vector size).

It's worth noting that the N100 (Intel Gracemont) implements 256-bit AVX on 128-bit units, so it doesn't actually have wider processing width than the Apple M chips.

---

Edit: it's also worth pointing out that `(x | ~y) ^ z` can be rewritten as `~((~x & y) ^ z)` or `-((~x & y) ^ z) - 1`.  The '-1' can be coded into the constant, and the result of F subtracted instead of added (to subsume the negation).  This is particularly useful on x86 which lacks a ORN equivalent.
